content:
I'll be the first to admit that my modified iPhone camera setup looks pretty ridiculous — but it has actually made my iPhone photography more useful, and more enjoyable.

This modification originally came about as a way to solve a problem I was having while filming a particular video, but then I found myself using it far more often than I expected…

One of the biggest distinctions in the world of compact cameras is whether or not they have a viewfinder. Old-school camera enthusiasts used to get very heated about the merits of electronic viewfinders (EVFs) versus optical ones, but EVFs are now so good that essentially nobody cares anymore.

But whether optical or electronic, a viewfinder offers very practical advantages over composing shots on the rear screen, especially when shooting in harsh sunlight. Even with screen brightness turned all the way up, it's hard to see what you're shooting in bright sun, and you may have to contend with reflections on the screen too.

In London, this has never really been a major issue, but this summer has brought record-breaking heatwaves, and honestly, I feel like the last time I saw a cloud or any rain was about thirty years ago.

But for me, there's more to it than that. I also feel that seeing only what's in the frame when you're composing a shot produces a different psychological feeling from seeing everything around you. Sometimes it's precisely that immersive quality that makes me reach for a dedicated camera instead of my iPhone.

When I was choosing a camera for video work a few years ago, the Blackmagic Pocket Cinema Camera 4K was clearly the top choice at the time, but I did hesitate over its lack of a viewfinder. In the end I decided it wasn't a deal-breaker for me, since I'd mainly be using it indoors, and for outdoor use I could attach a larger screen with a sun hood to solve most of the problem.

But there were times when I wanted to use it without lugging around the whole rig with the monitor, so I found a simple accessory suitable for outdoor use. It's a two-in-one sun hood and magnifier that attaches magnetically to the camera's rear screen, effectively giving you an optical viewfinder.

I had an upcoming shoot where I'd be filming with both the BMPCC 4K and my iPhone 16 Pro Max. I did a quick test shoot on location and found the viewfinder accessory really did help. Since the BMPCC 4K and iPhone screens are fairly similar in size, I wondered if the accessory might also work on the iPhone.

Of course, the iPhone doesn't have a magnetic mounting system, but the iPhone is light enough that holding it manually against the magnifier isn't an issue at all. To my surprise, this worked brilliantly — especially when using the Camera Control button as a shutter.

Since then, I've found myself reaching for it in quite a few situations, enjoying the easier screen visibility in harsh sunlight, and that immersive feeling. My iPhone has been my main camera for a few years now, and with this DIY modification I feel even more confident that there are many occasions when the phone alone is more than enough.

Idiot or genius? Let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you agree with the latter, unfortunately the product I bought seems to have been discontinued, and I haven't seen anything similar designed for screens larger than three inches. If you find one, drop a link in the comments.
